sections.title: Generating a QR Code
sections.extract: This page is a step-by-step, implementer-facing walkthrough of how a signed health certificate becomes a QR code on a piece of paper or a phone screen, and how a verifier turns that QR code back into trustworthy data. The container, the signature and the transport encoding are the same for every GDHCN trust domain, and are specified normatively in the HCERT Specification. What changes from one use case to the next

sections.title: 1. The pipeline at a glance
sections.extract: use case ──▶ logical model ──▶ hcert subclaim │ Step 1 Select payload type ──────────────────────────────┘ Step 2 Assemble payload { "n": ..., "dob": ..., "vx": {...} } Step 3 Wrap in CWT claim set { 1: iss, 6: iat, 4: exp, -260: { -6: payload } } Step 4 Serialise as CBOR binary Step 5 Sign as COSE_Sign1 (ES256) binary, tag 18 Step 6 Compress with ZLIB/Deflate binary Step 7 Encode as Base45 ASCII Step 8 Prefix

sections.title: 2. Step 1 — Select the logical model for your use case
sections.extract: An HCERT carries exactly one payload, identified by a subclaim inside the hcert claim (-260). Choosing the subclaim is choosing the data model, and the choice follows from the use case, not from the technology.

sections.title: 2.1 Subclaims defined in this guide
sections.extract: These are the subclaims enumerated by the HCert logical model. Section 3.2.7.1 of the HCERT Specification remains authoritative. Subclaim; Logical model; Carries; Status 1; HCertDCC; EU Digital Covid Certificate core data set; Assigned 3; DDCCCoreDataSetVS; DDCC vaccination status; Proposed 4; DDCCCoreDataSetTR; DDCC test result; Proposed 5; string; URI of a Verifiable Health Link (VHL); Assigned -6; DVCMin; Minimal

sections.title: 2.2 Choosing between a DVC and a VHL
sections.extract: The decisive question is **whether the data must survive offline, and how much of it there is**. DVC in the QR (subclaim -6); VHL in the QR (subclaim 5) What the QR holds; The vaccination data itself, signed; A link to the data, signed Works fully offline; Yes — verifier needs only the trust list; No — verifier must dereference the link Data volume; Small, bounded; one immunization event per certificate; Unbounded;

sections.title: 2.3 Choosing between a generic DVC and the ICVP
sections.extract: The ICVP is the digital counterpart of the "Yellow Book" — the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis under the International Health Regulations. Its scope is deliberately narrow: the vaccinations and prophylaxis that may be required as a condition of entry, principally yellow fever. The generic DVC is for everything else: routine childhood immunization, national schedule doses, catch-up campaigns.

sections.title: 2.4 Decision summary
sections.extract: Is the certificate proving an IHR entry requirement (e.g. yellow fever)? ├── yes ──▶ ICVP trust domain └── no │ Does the content fit in a QR and have to verify with no network? ├── yes ──▶ DVC payload, hcert subclaim -6 (DVCMin / DVCMinPreQual) └── no ──▶ VHL URI, hcert subclaim 5 COVID-19 vaccination and test results predate this split and have their own assigned subclaims (3 and 4) under the DDCC trust domain.

sections.title: 3. Step 2 — Assemble the payload
sections.extract: Populate the logical model you selected. The DVC payload uses short element names because every byte is paid for twice: once in the CBOR encoding and again in the QR's module count. For DVCMin: Element; Card.; Meaning n; 1..1; Legal name of the patient, first and last dob; 1..1; Date of birth s; 1..1; Sex nt; 1..1; Nationality, ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 id; 0..1; National identification document number dt; 0..1; National

sections.title: 4. Step 3 — Build the CWT claim set
sections.extract: Place the payload under its subclaim, inside the hcert claim, inside a CWT claim set: Claim key; Name; Notes 1; iss; Issuer. Optionally the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code of the issuing country 6; iat; Issued At, integer NumericDate. MUST NOT predate the DSC validity period 4; exp; Expiration Time, integer NumericDate. MUST NOT exceed the DSC validity period -260; hcert; Map whose single key is the subclaim chosen in Step

sections.title: 5. Step 4 — Serialise as CBOR
sections.extract: Encode the claim set as CBOR (RFC 7049). The JSON shown throughout this page and in the logical models is schema notation only — the wire format is CBOR, and an implementation need never produce the JSON form at all. Strings SHOULD be NFC-normalised. Decoders SHOULD be permissive about input that is not.

sections.title: 6. Step 5 — Sign as a COSE_Sign1
sections.extract: Wrap the CBOR payload in a single-signer COSE structure (RFC 8152), CBOR tag 18. Protected header Label; Name; Value 1; alg; -7 for ES256 (primary) or -37 for PS256 (secondary) 4; kid; Key identifier of the Document Signing Certificate Both algorithms MUST be implemented, even though only one is used to sign any given certificate; the secondary exists so that a break in the primary does not strand the whole network.

sections.title: 7. Step 6 — Compress
sections.extract: Compress the COSE structure with ZLIB (RFC 1950) using Deflate (RFC 1951). Compression comes after signing, so the verifier decompresses before it verifies.

sections.title: 8. Step 7 — Encode as Base45
sections.extract: Encode the compressed bytes with Base45. Base45 exists for one reason: its 45-character alphabet is exactly the QR Alphanumeric character set, which stores data far more densely than byte mode.

sections.title: 9. Step 8 — Prefix the context identifier
sections.extract: Prefix the Base45 string with HC1:. Verifiers use this to recognise what they have scanned and which decoding scheme to apply. A future backwards-incompatible revision will use a new identifier, incrementing through [1-9] and then [A-Z].

sections.title: 10. Step 9 — Render the QR code
sections.extract: Property; Requirement Symbology; QR Code, ISO/IEC 18004:2015 — SHALL Encoding mode; Alphanumeric (Mode 2, symbols 0010) — MUST, in conjunction with Base45 Error correction; Level Q, approximately 25% — RECOMMENDED Rendered size; 35 mm to 60 mm diagonal — RECOMMENDED If you are printing below 300 dpi, make sure each module is rendered as an exact square. sections.title: 11. Verifying: the same steps upwards
sections.extract: 1. Confirm the HC1: prefix and strip it. 2. Base45-decode, then ZLIB-decompress. 3. Parse the COSE_Sign1 and read alg and kid from the protected header. 4. Validate the input before trusting it. Parsing the protected header necessarily happens before signature verification, which makes it an attack surface; check types and lengths defensively. See section 6.3. 5. Look the kid up on the trust list, retrieving every

sections.title: 12. Worked example — a newborn birth dose DVC
sections.extract: The following example is generated by the reference script in section 13, and every figure quoted here is taken from its output.

sections.title: 12.1 Scenario
sections.extract: A family from the Lao People's Democratic Republic is visiting relatives abroad when the mother delivers. The newborn receives the routine birth-dose vaccinations of the host country's national childhood immunization schedule before discharge. The clinic records the doses and issues a signed certificate; the family has one shared phone between them, so the clinic prints a paper card with the QR code and offers

sections.title: 12.2 Host-country schedule
sections.extract: Thailand's Expanded Programme on Immunization gives two vaccines at birth: **BCG as soon as possible after birth, and the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth**. The DTP-HepB and OPV series begin later, at 2, 4 and 6 months. A birth visit in Thailand therefore produces exactly the two certificates modelled here. Implementers should confirm the current schedule against the national authority

sections.title: 12.3 Test issuer
sections.extract: The example is issued by the GDHCN test participant XXA, not by any Member State. GDHCN participant codes are ISO 3166-1 alpha-3, while the CWT iss claim and the X.509 country attribute take the alpha-2 form, here the user-assigned code XX. The signing keys are throw-away test keys generated deterministically by the script. They appear on no trust list, and nothing signed with them verifies anywhere. In a real

sections.extract: Hepatitis B birth dose, hcert subclaim -6, shown in JSON notation: { "n": "Chanthala SOUVANNALATH", "dob": "2026-09-28", "s": "female", "nt": "LAO", "gn": "Mali SOUVANNALATH", "vx": { "vp": "XM9V38", "dv": "2026-09-28", "cn": "Dr Pimchanok WATTANA", "is": "org-xxa-provincial-hospital", "bo": "HEPB-2026-0914" }, "v": "1.0.0" } vp is ICD-11 XM9V38 Hepatitis B, purified antigen; the BCG certificate uses XM8142

sections.title: 12.5 Size at each stage
sections.extract: Stage; Size CWT claim set, CBOR; 210 bytes COSE_Sign1, signed; 295 bytes ZLIB/Deflate compressed; 282 bytes Base45 + HC1: prefix; 427 characters QR symbol; Version 16, error correction Q, Alphanumeric mode The signature and its headers account for 85 of the 295 bytes — on payloads this small, the cryptography costs more than the clinical data. sections.title: 13. Reference script
sections.extract: input/scripts/generate_dvc_qr.py in this guide's source repository implements every step on this page and regenerates the example above byte for byte: pip install cbor2 base45 qrcode pillow cryptography python3 input/scripts/generate_dvc_qr.py --out-dir input/images The script builds the test SCA and DSC, derives the kid, assembles both DVC payloads, signs, compresses, encodes and renders — and then decodes its own
